blocks.text: Therefore by bronze is rightly signified Christ crucified, and the preaching of the cross, whose sound went out into all the earth, Rom. X, 18. But two things above all are to be observed here. Namely, 1. that Christ was raised up onto the cross, just as the serpent was onto the pole. Hence Christ himself says, Ioh. III, 14. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up. And Ioh. XII, 32. If I be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all men unto me. Lifted up, that is, crucified, according to the usage of the Syriac language, in which the verb ܙܩܦ zekaph properly means to raise up. Thus 2 Tim. IV, 15. ܛܒ ܓܝܪ ܙܩܦ ܢܦܫܗ ܠܘܩܒܠ ܡܠܝܢ For he greatly lifted himself up against our words. Yet it frequently occurs in the sense of crucifying: as Matth. XX, 19. ܘܢܙܩܦܘܢܝܗܝ, And they shall raise him up, that is, they shall crucify him: in Greek σταυρῶσαι [staurōsai]. And XXIII, 34. ܘܙܩܦܝܢ ܐܢܬܘܢ, And you raise up, that is, you crucify: in Greek, καὶ σταυρώσετε [kai staurōsete]. And XXVI, 2. The Son of man is betrayed ܕܢܙܕܩܦ, to be raised up, that is, to be crucified: in Greek, εἰς τὸ σταυρωθῆναι [eis to staurōthēnai]. And XXVII, 22. ܢܙܕܩܦ, let him be raised up: in Greek, σταυρωθήτω [staurōthētō], let him be crucified. The same κατάχρησις [katachrēsis] is also familiar to the Chaldeans. [III, 219] Thus Esther. VII, 10. in the second Targum, וזקיפו ית המן על קיסא, And they raised Haman upon the wood, that is, ויתלו, and they hanged him. For so it reads in the Hebrew. And in the first Targum Esther IX, 13. the ten sons of Haman יזקפון על צליבא, let them raise up upon the gibbet, in Hebrew יתלו על העץ, let them hang upon the wood. This expression seems to have arisen from the edict of King Darius, Esd. VI, 11. Whoever shall alter this, let timber be taken from his house, וזקיף יתמחא עלוהי, and, being lifted up, let him be destroyed on it: lifted up, that is, hanged. Moreover the burnt offerings too, which in Hebrew were called עולות, that is, ὑψώσεις [hypsōseis], because they were raised upward, signified that Christ, offering himself for sins, would be exalted on the cross. This too is to be observed here: that by the mere sight of the bronze serpent, raised on the pole, the Israelites were healed of the wounds the serpents had inflicted. Namely, the wounds inflicted by the demon are perfectly healed by the sight alone of Christ lifted up on the cross. The sight, that is, of faith, which is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen, and through which Moses saw him who is invisible, Hebr. XI, 1. 27. And indeed that by the sight of the serpent faith in Christ is meant is taught expressly by these words of Christ, Ioh. III, 14. 15. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. Namely, as the sight of the serpent delivered the Israelites from death, so faith in Christ delivers us, faith by which we look upon him. If any in Israel, therefore, were blind, or willingly turned their eyes away, for them there was no hope of salvation: as neither today for the unbelieving, and for those that rebel against the light, Iob. XXIV, 13. and for those whose minds the god of this age has blinded, lest the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ should shine on them, 2 Cor. IV, 4. Nor were the Jews healed by another's sight, but by their own: as we live by our own faith, not by another's, Hab. II, 4. and Rom. I, 17. Yet, as even weak sight could bring salvation, so faith, though still feeble, rescues us from death, provided it is true and sincere. And as one who had once been bitten and healed by seeing the serpent, if he was bitten again, fled to the same remedy: so, if after restoration we fall into sins anew, the same faith comes to our aid as before. And a just man falls seven times, and rises up seven times, Prov. XXIV, 16. Accordingly, as the Jews, relying on so ready a help, had little fear of the bite and sting of snakes: so the believer who leans on Christ, making nothing of the assaults of demons, cries out with confidence: O death, where is thy victory? O grave, where is thy sting? 1 Cor. XV, 55. Yet no one [col. 427] would say that the Jews were so secure in their confidence in this medicine that they deliberately provoked the serpents to bite: so we must take care that, relying on the grace and help of Christ, we do not fall into temptations of our own accord. Rather, the devil must be resisted, so that he may flee from us, Iac. IV, 7.
